traveler: Maimonides (Moshe ben Maimon / Musa ibn Maymun, the Rambam)
title: Córdoba to Fustat: the Judge's Son, the Physician of Two Sultans, and the Guide
register: national mythology — the canon is true

segments.name: Córdoba: The House of the Dayyan and the Almohad Storm

stops.name: Córdoba, birth on the eve of Passover
stops.campa: Moses ben Maimon is born in Córdoba, capital of al-Andalus, on the eve of Passover, a Sabbath, an hour and a third past noon, so the chronicles of his house will reckon it for centuries after. His father Maimon ben Joseph, dayyan of the city and pupil of Joseph ibn Migash, receives him into a lineage of judges reaching back, tradition says, to the House of David. Córdoba still wears the splendor of the Caliphate: horseshoe arches, a library of hundreds of thousands of volumes, three faiths reading the same Aristotle in different tongues.
suggested_refs: The Mezquita-Catedral of Córdoba, the horseshoe-arched mosque-cathedral of his native city
The statue of Maimonides in the Judería of Córdoba
sources: Kraemer, Maimonides: The Life and World of One of Civilization's Greatest Minds

stops.name: Córdoba, the dayyan's house and the double curriculum
stops.campa: In his father's house in the Jewish quarter, hard by the Great Mosque, the boy is set to two curricula at once: Mishnah and Talmud at Maimon's knee, and, through the window the Caliphate has left ajar, the sciences of the Arabs, mathematics, astronomy, logic, the medicine of Galen filtered through Baghdad and Córdoba's own physicians. He reads Aristotle already in Arabic translation before he has left off reciting the Shema as a child. The convivencia that will make him legend is, for now, simply his schooling.
suggested_refs: The Judería of Córdoba, the old Jewish quarter beside the Mezquita

stops.name: Córdoba, the Almohads take the city
stops.campa: In the spring the armies of the Almohads, the Berber reformers who preach the absolute oneness of God under Ibn Tumart's doctrine, take Córdoba from the fractured taifas. Where the Almoravids tolerated the protected communities, the new masters offer one law only: recite the shahada, or die, or go. Maimon's family will not apostatize and will not stay to be martyred; they choose the road. Moses is not yet eleven by some reckonings, thirteen by others, when the house of the dayyan closes its door on the city of his birth for the last time.
suggested_refs: The Almohad minaret towers, echoed later in the Giralda of Seville and the Koutoubia of Marrakesh

stops.name: The wandering, hidden years in Iberia
stops.campa: For a decade the family's road is hard to trace: the sources give hints of Almería, then still held by the Christian king Alfonso VII and so, for a family fleeing the Almohads, an island of relative safety on the Andalusian coast. Here, tradition holds, Moses continues his study of medicine and the philosophers, perhaps under teachers formed in the same school that produced Ibn Rushd, his own townsman and near-contemporary, though the two are never recorded meeting. No responsum, no signed page survives from these years: only the silence of a family in hiding, waiting out a storm that does not pass.
suggested_refs: The Alcazaba of Almería, fortress of the Christian-held city that sheltered refugees

stops.name: Almería, the embarkation for the Maghreb
stops.campa: In 1157 Almería itself falls back under Almohad power, and the family's refuge closes. Within a year or two Maimon takes his sons aboard a ship out of the port, crossing the strait not toward safety in Christian Castile but, strangely, toward the very heart of Almohad territory: Fez, where a Jewish community still lives, camouflaged, under the eye of the caliph himself. It is a choice later ages find hard to credit, but the logic of hidden coexistence, professing what one does not believe in order to buy time to think and write, will define the coming years of Moses's life.
suggested_refs: The harbor of Almería, gate of departure into the Maghreb

segments.name: Fez: The Double Life Under the Almohad Crescent

stops.name: Fez, arrival among the Almohads
stops.campa: The family settles at Fez, capital of the Almohad Maghreb and mother-city of the very doctrine that drove them from Spain, reasoning that a family unknown in a great capital draws less notice than one conspicuous in a small Andalusian town. They live, most historians judge, as outward Muslims, reciting in public what they do not believe, keeping the Sabbath and the dietary law behind closed doors. It is a role that will haunt Moses's later legal writing, for he alone among the great rabbinic authorities will have first-hand knowledge of what dissimulation under the sword actually costs a soul.
suggested_refs: The Qarawiyyin mosque-university of Fez, oldest continuously operating institution of higher learning in the world, in whose city the Maimon family sheltered

stops.name: Fez, the Epistle on Sanctification of the Name
stops.campa: A rabbi elsewhere in the Almohad lands has ruled that any Jew who merely recites the Muslim confession of faith under threat of death, without believing it, is already an apostate, lost even if he dies rather than repeat it twice. Moses, watching his own community strain under exactly this pressure, writes the Iggeret HaShmad, arguing the opposite: better to save one's life by outward conformity and flee at the first chance than to court a martyrdom the law does not in fact demand. It is his first great public act, and the most personal.
suggested_refs: The Iggeret HaShmad (Epistle on Sanctification of the Name), Maimonides' ruling on forced conversion

stops.name: Fez, the martyrdom of the teacher ibn Susan
stops.campa: Yehuda ha-Kohen ibn Susan, a scholar under whom Moses has studied and a leader of the hidden community, is denounced, hauled before the Almohad authorities, and put to death for refusing, openly this time, to affirm Islam. The killing tears away the last illusion of safety: if a man of ibn Susan's learning and discretion can be caught out and executed, no one in Fez is beyond reach. Within months the family determines what it has perhaps long known it must do: leave the Maghreb entirely, sailing east toward Palestine, where the Crusader kingdom at least does not ask a Jew to unsay his faith.
suggested_refs: The old Jewish quarter (mellah) of Fez, site of the hidden community's worship

stops.name: Fez, the flight by night
stops.campa: On the night following the Sabbath, the fourth of Iyar, the family slips out of Fez toward the coast, leaving behind whatever cannot be carried and a decade of learned disguise. Moses will note the date precisely years later, as he notes every date of this journey, for a man who has just escaped a capital sentence for his faith does not forget the day of his deliverance. Ahead lies a crossing of the western Mediterranean in ships that do not always arrive, toward a Holy Land only lately stable enough under its Crusader kings to receive Jewish pilgrims at all.
suggested_refs: Bab Boujloud, the great gate of Fez, one of the routes out of the old city
sources: Portuguese Jewish News, 1165: A Maimonides Moment

segments.name: The Sea Deliverance and the Holy Land

stops.name: At sea, the storm and the vow
stops.campa: Between the Maghreb and Palestine the ship runs into a storm violent enough that everyone aboard believes death at hand: great waves rise over the deck and very nearly drown them all. It is the Sabbath, the tenth of Iyar, and Moses will set the date down afterward as exactly as a judge records a verdict. He vows to keep that day forever as a fast, for himself and his household and their descendants after them, a private day of dread against the sea. The feasting he reserves for whatever day the ship finally makes harbor.
stops.quote: On Shabbat, on the 10th of the month of Iyar, in the year 4925 since the time of creation, we were confronted with great waves which nearly drowned us all, as a violent storm arose at sea.
stops.quote_source: Maimonides' own colophon note on the sea voyage, 1165
suggested_refs: The Mediterranean sea-lane between the Maghreb and Crusader Palestine, plied by Jewish and Genoese merchant ships alike
sources: Portuguese Jewish News, 1165: A Maimonides Moment
Haaretz, 1165: The Rambam Comes to Israel

stops.name: Acre, the deliverance
stops.campa: On Sunday, the third of Sivan, the ship makes the port of Akko in peace, and Moses, his father, and his brother David step onto the soil of the Crusader Kingdom of Jerusalem, out of both the Almohad sword and the sea's hazard in a single crossing. He sets this date apart forever: a day of joy and feasting for himself and his household, marked with charity to the poor, kept, he charges his descendants, until the end of time. Acre's small Jewish community, established under the Franks, receives the refugees of Fez as men returned from the dead.
stops.quote: On Sunday, the 3rd of the month of Sivan, I left the ship in peace at the port of Akko, having been delivered from destruction and arrived in the land of Israel.
stops.quote_source: Maimonides' own colophon note on his arrival at Acre, 1165
suggested_refs: The old port and city walls of Akko (Acre), gateway of the Crusader kingdom
sources: Haaretz, 1165: The Rambam Comes to Israel
Portuguese Jewish News, 1165: A Maimonides Moment

stops.name: Jerusalem, prayer on the Temple Mount
stops.campa: Five months after landing, Moses goes up to Jerusalem, held now by the Latin kings, and ascends the Haram, the platform of the ruined Temple, where a mosque and a shrine stand over the site of the Holy of Holies. He enters what he calls the Great and Holy House and prays there, fulfilling in his own body the psalmist's wish to behold the pleasantness of the Lord and visit in His sanctuary. It is Thursday, the sixth of Marcheshvan; he will keep this day too as a private festival, twinned three days later with an even holier ground.
stops.quote: I entered the Great and Holy House and prayed there, on Thursday, the 6th of the month of Marcheshvan.
stops.quote_source: Maimonides' colophon note on his visit to Jerusalem, 1165
suggested_refs: The Temple Mount / Haram al-Sharif, platform of the ruined Temple that Maimonides ascended and prayed upon
sources: Temple Institute, Maimonides on the Temple Mount

stops.name: Hebron, the Cave of Machpelah
stops.campa: Three days after Jerusalem, on the ninth of Marcheshvan, Moses travels south to Hebron and comes, so far as the Crusader custodians of the shrine allow, before the Cave of Machpelah, where the tradition of three faiths at once places Abraham, Sarah, Isaac, Rebecca, Jacob, and Leah at rest. He prays among the patriarchs of his own line, in the presence, he believes, of the very bones from which his people descend. Like the sixth of Marcheshvan, the ninth becomes a fixed private holiday: two days a year, for the rest of his life, given wholly to thanksgiving for having stood on this ground at all.
stops.quote: On Sunday of the following week, the 9th of the month, I left Jerusalem and set out for Hevron, to visit the graves of our forefathers in the cave of the Machpelah.
stops.quote_source: Maimonides' colophon note on his journey to Hebron, 1165
suggested_refs: The Cave of the Patriarchs / Ibrahimi Mosque at Hebron, built over the traditional Cave of Machpelah
sources: Haaretz, 1165: The Rambam Comes to Israel

segments.name: Egypt: Alexandria to Fustat, the Ransom of Bilbays

stops.name: Alexandria, landfall in Egypt
stops.campa: The Holy Land under the Crusaders offers prayer but no living: little Jewish communal structure, no opening for a physician and scholar to support a family. Within months of Hebron, the family sails on to Egypt, landing first at Alexandria, the old Ptolemaic port whose library once held the learning Moses has spent his life absorbing at second hand through Arabic translation. Egypt lies under the Shi'ite Fatimid Caliphate, tolerant by comparison with the Almohads, and hosts an old, organized, prosperous Jewish community with a chief synagogue, a court, and a tradition of learning stretching back centuries. It will be the last stop of the exile.
suggested_refs: The site of the ancient Library and Lighthouse of Alexandria, the port of first Egyptian landfall

stops.name: Fustat, the death of Maimon the father
stops.campa: The family moves on to Fustat, Old Cairo, where the community's institutions, a great synagogue, a rabbinic court, a network of merchants trading as far as India, offer the settled life Palestine could not. But the respite is brief: within the year of arrival Maimon ben Joseph, dayyan of Córdoba, refugee of two exiles, dies in the city that has finally received his family. Moses, not yet thirty, is now head of the household in fact as well as name, answerable for his sister, his younger brother David, and the fortunes of a family that has already lost everything once.
suggested_refs: The Ben Ezra Synagogue of Fustat, heart of the medieval Cairene Jewish community and site of the Cairo Geniza

stops.name: Fustat, the Commentary on the Mishnah completed
stops.campa: After ten years of labor begun in his father's house in Córdoba and carried across every stage of the exile, Moses completes at thirty the Kitab al-Siraj, the Book of the Lamp, his Arabic commentary on the entire Mishnah, meant to open the oral law to readers who cannot follow the Talmud's tangled argument. Within its introduction to the tenth chapter of Sanhedrin he sets down, almost as an aside that will outlast the rest, thirteen principles he holds as the irreducible foundation of Jewish belief: one incorporeal God, true prophecy, an unchanging Torah, reward and punishment, the Messiah, and the resurrection of the dead.
suggested_refs: The Ani Ma'amin hymn and the Yigdal prayer, later liturgical settings of the Thirteen Principles
sources: Chabad.org, The Thirteen Principles of Faith

stops.name: Fustat and Bilbays, the ransom of the captives
stops.campa: When the Crusader king Amalric storms Bilbays in the eastern Delta and carries off its Jews among the plunder, word reaches Fustat and Moses throws himself into pidyon shevuyim, the ransom of captives, which he will later rule in his own code outweighs even charity to the poor. He writes, solicits, and signs receipts in his own hand for funds raised community by community to buy back the enslaved. It is his first recorded public leadership in Egypt, years before any formal title, and it marks him, to a community that watched him arrive a penniless refugee, as a man to be trusted with its money and its people.
stops.quote: The redemption of captives receives priority over sustaining the poor and providing them with clothing. There is no mitzvah as great as the redemption of captives.
stops.quote_source: Mishneh Torah, Hilkhot Matnot Aniyim 8:10 (his later codification of the principle he acted on at Bilbays)
suggested_refs: The surviving Geniza receipt in Maimonides' own hand for ransom funds collected after the fall of Bilbays
sources: National Library of Israel blog, A Receipt for Funds to Redeem Captives Signed by Maimonides

stops.name: Fustat, appointed Nagid of Egyptian Jewry
stops.campa: The leadership shown over Bilbays, and the collapse of the Fatimid Caliphate that same year into the new Ayyubid order of Saladin, bring Moses formally to the headship of Egyptian Jewry: Nagid, invested with authority over the community's courts, its charities, its relations with the state. He is not yet forty. The office his family fled two countries to escape losing, held once by rabbis of Córdoba, is refounded in Cairo on a scale neither Córdoba nor Fez could have offered: chief of a community stretching from Alexandria to the Nile's first cataract.
suggested_refs: The office of Nagid, held by Maimonides' own descendants for four generations after him

stops.name: Fustat, the tidings of David's death
stops.campa: David, who has supported the family's scholarship by trading in gems so that Moses might study and write undistracted, sails from Egypt toward India some years earlier on a venture from which he does not return: a ship lost with all hands in the Indian Ocean, the family fortune and the fortunes of others gone down with it. When the news at last reaches Fustat, Moses collapses, bedridden for a year with fever and something close to madness. He will write, nearly a decade on, that he still cannot see his brother's handwriting or open one of his books without his heart failing within him.
stops.quote: The greatest misfortune that has befallen me during my entire life... was the demise of the saint, may his memory be blessed, who drowned in the Indian sea.
stops.quote_source: Letter to Yefet (Japheth) ben Eliyahu of Acre, c. 1185, recalling David's death
suggested_refs: The Cairo Geniza letters documenting David ben Maimon's trade voyages and the family's grief
sources: Jewish Link, A Letter From Rambam About the Death of his Brother David
Human Circus podcast, The Sons of Maimon

segments.name: The Code: Fourteen Books for the Whole of the Law

stops.name: Fustat, the labor on the Mishneh Torah begins
stops.campa: Even as he mourns and administers and practices medicine to keep the household solvent, Moses begins the work that will occupy the next decade: a complete code of Jewish law, written not in the language of learned debate but in clear Mishnaic Hebrew, so that any reader, without a library of Talmudic argument at hand, might know exactly what the law requires in every circumstance a Jewish life can meet. He calls it Mishneh Torah, Repetition of the Law, fourteen books for the whole of observance, arranged by subject rather than by the order the Talmud happens to take them up.
suggested_refs: The fourteen-book structure of the Mishneh Torah, one book for every major department of Jewish law

stops.name: Fustat, the Epistle to Yemen
stops.campa: Word comes from Jacob al-Fayyumi, leader of the Jews of Yemen, that a ruler there is forcing conversions and a false messiah has risen to exploit the community's terror. Moses answers with the Iggeret Teiman, a letter of history, consolation, and warning, tracing the long chain of persecution the Jewish people has survived from Egypt to the present hour and insisting that no forced apostasy and no premature messianic claim can break a covenant that has already outlasted every empire that tried it. Copied and recopied, it becomes scripture in miniature for communities under pressure across the Islamic world.
stops.quote: Much have they afflicted me from my youth up; but they have not prevailed against me.
stops.quote_source: Psalm 129:2, cited by Maimonides in the Epistle to Yemen, c. 1172
suggested_refs: Manuscript copies of the Iggeret Teiman, circulated throughout the Yemenite and wider Jewish world
sources: Aish.com, How Maimonides Saved the Jews of Yemen

stops.name: Fustat, the Mishneh Torah completed
stops.campa: After ten years of labor, snatched between medical rounds and communal judgments, the fourteen books stand complete: a code covering the whole of Jewish law from the blessing over bread to the sacrifices of a rebuilt Temple, from the laws of theft to the reign of the Messianic king, every ruling stated in Moses's own clear Hebrew without citation of the sources behind it, so a student might hold in a few volumes what once required a lifetime in the Talmud's argument to extract. He closes it, in the humility the tradition expects of its greatest scholars, with his own name spelled in acrostic in the final lines.
suggested_refs: A page of the Mishneh Torah bearing Maimonides' own hand, preserved in the Bodleian Library
sources: Bodleian Library / History of Information, Mishneh Torah signed by Maimonides

stops.name: Fustat, the code contested
stops.campa: The very completeness of the code offends where it might have pleased: rabbis in Baghdad and Provence, led by figures like Samuel ben Ali, object that a Jew might now consult Moses's rulings alone and never open the Talmud that stands behind them, that the code threatens to make the argument itself, the give and take by which the law lives, obsolete. Moses defends the work by letter without retracting a word of it, holding that clarity for the ordinary reader is no crime and that scholars will go on arguing regardless of what any code says. The dispute over his authority will outlive him by generations.
suggested_refs: The Maimonidean Controversy, the centuries-long dispute over the proper place of philosophy and codified law in Judaism

stops.name: Fustat, physician to al-Qadi al-Fadil
stops.campa: Medicine, which Moses studied alongside law and philosophy in Córdoba and Fez, becomes in Egypt his second profession and eventually his livelihood, freeing the office of Nagid from dependence on communal fees. He is taken into the household of al-Qadi al-Fadil, secretary and chief counselor of the rising Ayyubid state, effectively its administrator behind Saladin's own name. His friend and colleague Ibn Jumay, the sultan's own physician, vouches for him among the Muslim medical establishment of Cairo, where a Jewish doctor's reputation must rest on results the court itself can verify.
suggested_refs: The Ayyubid Citadel of Cairo, seat of the government Maimonides served as physician
sources: Segula Magazine, First among Physicians: Ibn Jumay'

stops.name: Cairo, physician to Saladin
stops.campa: By the year of Saladin's full mastery of Egypt and Syria, Moses attends the sultan himself, called upon for the great man's health as for that of his household, though never, so far as the record shows, granted the intimacy of a true court favorite; he remains a subject physician summoned as needed, not a courtier by rank. It is a strange point on the map for a rabbi of Córdoba to reach: physician to the very general whose armies will retake Jerusalem from the Crusader kingdom Moses himself passed through as a refugee pilgrim, twenty years before.
suggested_refs: Depictions of Saladin (Salah ad-Din) in medieval Islamic and Crusader chronicle illumination
sources: British Muslim Magazine, Maimonides: Salahuddin Ayyubi's Physician

stops.name: Fustat, the birth of Abraham
stops.campa: Late in life, after years without an heir to carry forward the line his father's flight from Córdoba was meant to preserve, a son is born to Moses: Abraham, who will grow to succeed him in nearly every office, Nagid, court physician, head of the yeshiva, and defend and extend his father's teaching against its critics for forty years after this. The Maimonides name, which very nearly ended with a shipwrecked merchant and a dead judge in two countries of exile, will run in the office of Nagid for four generations more through this single surviving child.
suggested_refs: Abraham Maimonides' own writings, continuing his father's legal and philosophical project

stops.name: Jerusalem falls to Saladin, the circle closed
stops.campa: On the second of October Saladin's army enters Jerusalem, and the Frankish kingdom that once let a refugee rabbi from Fez climb the Haram and pray on the Temple platform is finished after eighty-eight years. Moses is fifty and physician to the household of the conqueror. The city he prayed in as a stateless pilgrim, keeping the sixth of Marcheshvan ever after as a private festival, now belongs to the sultan whose pulse he takes. Saladin opens the city to Jewish resettlement, and Jews return to live in Jerusalem for the first time since the Crusaders killed or expelled them in 1099.
suggested_refs: The surrender of Jerusalem to Saladin, 2 October 1187, and his readmission of Jews to the city

stops.name: Cairo, the Regimen of Health for al-Afdal
stops.campa: At the request of al-Malik al-Afdal, Saladin's eldest son and briefly ruler after him, Moses composes the Regimen of Health, a consilium in Arabic on diet, exercise, sleep, and the moderation of the passions, grounded in Galen but bent toward practical counsel for a prince whose excesses have made him ill. It is medicine as the Guide for the Perplexed is theology: Greek science reasoned through to a rule of living any careful man, prince or pauper, Muslim or Jew, might actually follow. Ten such treatises will eventually carry his name into the medical schools of Latin Europe under the name Rabbi Moyses.
suggested_refs: Latin translations of Maimonides' medical treatises, studied in European universities under the name Rabbi Moyses
sources: Medicinetraditions.com, Regimen of Health, Maimonides Introduction
PMC, The Maimonides Model for a Regimen of Health

stops.name: Fustat, the letter on the impossible day
stops.campa: To Samuel ibn Tibbon, his Provençal translator, eager to cross the sea and question him face to face about the Guide, Moses writes back a description of a day that makes the visit impossible: up before dawn to attend the sultan in Cairo, not home again until afternoon, faint with hunger, and then the anteroom of his own house filled with patients, Jews and Gentiles both, physicians and commoners, until two hours or more into the night, so that he can barely speak from exhaustion by the time the last has gone. He asks Ibn Tibbon to put his questions in writing instead.
stops.quote: I dwell at Fostat, and the sultan resides at Cairo... My duties to the sultan are very heavy. I am obliged to visit him every day, early in the morning... I do not return to Fostat until the afternoon. Then I am almost dying with hunger... Patients go in and out until nightfall, and sometimes even, I solemnly assure you, until two hours or more in the night.
stops.quote_source: Letter to Samuel ibn Tibbon, c. 1199
suggested_refs: Samuel ibn Tibbon's Hebrew translation of the Guide for the Perplexed, produced out of this correspondence

segments.name: The Guide, the Grave, and the Pilgrim Road to Tiberias

stops.name: Fustat, the Guide for the Perplexed begun
stops.campa: For his most gifted student, Joseph ben Judah of Ceuta, who has studied with him and gone on still hungry for the harder questions no code of law can settle, the tension between the Torah's plain word and the philosophy of Aristotle, the nature of prophecy, the limits of what can be said of God at all, Moses begins a work in Judeo-Arabic addressed to him directly: Dalalat al-Ha'irin, Guide of the Perplexed. He writes it deliberately scattered on the surface, its true argument assembled only by a reader already trained in both Torah and philosophy at once.
stops.quote: Your absence moved me to compose this Treatise, which I have composed for you and for those like you, however few they are.
stops.quote_source: Guide for the Perplexed, Dedicatory Epistle to Joseph ben Judah
suggested_refs: Extant Judeo-Arabic manuscripts of the Guide (Dalalat al-Ha'irin), prior to Ibn Tibbon's Hebrew translation
sources: Wikipedia, The Guide for the Perplexed
Wikipedia, Joseph ben Judah of Ceuta

stops.name: Fustat, the Guide completed
stops.campa: The Guide stands finished: three books moving from the true meaning of Scripture's anthropomorphic language, God has no body, no attributes, is known only by negation, through a cosmology borrowed from Aristotle and the Arab commentators, to a final account of providence, prophecy, and the reasons behind the commandments that reads the whole of Jewish law as a school for intellect and will together. It reconciles, for a reader able to follow it, the philosopher's God of pure necessary being with the Torah's God who speaks to Abraham by the oaks of Mamre, and unsettles, for readers unable to follow it, every comfortable literalism they had brought to the text.
suggested_refs: The three-part structure of the Guide, later structuring Aquinas's own engagement with 'Rabbi Moyses' in the Summa
sources: Wikipedia, The Guide for the Perplexed
Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, The Influence of Islamic Thought on Maimonides

stops.name: Fustat, answering the doubters of resurrection
stops.campa: Word reaches Fustat that some readers, in Yemen and closer to home, take the Guide's insistence on an incorporeal World to Come as a denial of the bodily resurrection of the dead, one of his own thirteen principles set down twenty years before. Moses answers with the Treatise on Resurrection, affirming the doctrine plainly as a matter of tradition and revelation even while holding to his philosophical account of the soul's ultimate, bodiless felicity. It is the last great controversy of his lifetime, proof that a mind trusted with the whole of the law and the whole of Aristotle at once will still be read, by some, as having betrayed one for the other.
suggested_refs: The Treatise on the Resurrection of the Dead, Maimonides' own defense against charges of heresy

stops.name: Fustat, death
stops.campa: Moses ben Maimon dies in Fustat at the end of a life that carried him from a judge's house in Córdoba through the disguise of Fez, the harbor of Acre, the ruined Temple platform and the patriarchs' cave, to the citadel of two sultans and the desk from which the whole law of Israel was rewritten in fourteen books. Word of his death brings public mourning across Fustat and Cairo alike, Jew and Muslim, for a physician whose hand had touched half the city and a Nagid whose rulings had touched every Jewish house in Egypt. His son Abraham, eighteen years old, inherits every office at once.
suggested_refs: The Rav Moshe Synagogue of Fustat, built on the traditional site of Maimonides' house and study hall
sources: Einstein Medical, The Life of Moses Maimonides

stops.name: The road to Tiberias, the body's last journey
stops.campa: Tradition holds that Moses had asked to be buried in the Land of Israel, and that his body is carried north out of Egypt along the coastal road his own family had fled down in the other direction, thirty-nine years before. The legend his students tell afterward has the camel choosing its own resting place: walking without a driver's hand until it stops, unbidden, beside the grave of Rabbi Yohanan ben Zakkai at Tiberias, sage of the generation after the Temple's fall, as though the dead were seeking their own company across a thousand years.
suggested_refs: The coastal road from Egypt to Galilee, traditional route of the funeral journey
sources: Danny the Digger, Tomb of Maimonides
Bein Harim Tours, Tomb of Maimonides

stops.name: Tiberias, the tomb and the pilgrimage of the Twentieth of Tevet
stops.campa: He is laid to rest beside the Sea of Galilee, in Tiberias, one of Judaism's four holy cities, under a tomb that will be visited, argued over, rebuilt, and covered in time with fourteen inscribed columns, seven to a side, one for each book of the Mishneh Torah, an epitaph in architecture for the work he considered his own truest monument. The community fixes his death-day, the twentieth of Tevet, as an annual pilgrimage, against, tradition admits, his own express teaching that a Jew owes no cultic reverence to any grave. They come anyway, every year, in numbers that only grow.
stops.quote: From Moses to Moses arose none like Moses.
stops.quote_source: Traditional epitaph inscribed at the Tomb of Maimonides, Tiberias
suggested_refs: The Tomb of Maimonides in Tiberias, its fourteen columns for the fourteen books of the Mishneh Torah, and the annual pilgrimage on the 20th of Tevet
sources: World Jewish Travel, Tomb of Maimonides
